ardent

/AR-duhnt/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Ardent means burning with intense, steady enthusiasm or devotion — passion that holds its heat over time.

Rosa's ardent defense of the town's oldest oak filled three city-council meetings with hand-drawn petitions.

Example

For three years, Jonah has spent nearly every Saturday pulling invasive buckthorn from the two acres of prairie behind the fairgrounds. He reads seed catalogs at lunch, budgets his allowance for bluestem plugs, and talks about root depths with anyone who stands still long enough. His scoutmaster put it simply: plenty of volunteers are reliable, but Jonah's devotion to that prairie is ardent — three years in, the fire hasn't dropped a degree.

What makes Jonah ardent rather than merely dutiful is the heat: dawn Saturdays, unprompted enthusiasm, and an intensity that has stayed lit for years. Ardent names devotion you can feel burning.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

devoted: Devoted means loyally committed over time — a devoted volunteer shows up, year after year. Ardent adds the heat: an ardent volunteer doesn't just show up, they burn for the work, and you can feel the warmth the moment they start talking about it.

passionate: Passionate means moved by strong emotion, and passion can flare up and fade just as fast. Ardent is passion that holds its temperature — a steady, burning devotion to one person, cause, or pursuit that is still hot years later.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

indifferent: not caring one way or the other

lukewarm: barely interested; half-hearted

Where it sits · how hot the devotion burns

keen → ardent → zealous

keen vs. ardent: Keen is weaker than ardent: a keen student shows eager, bright interest, while ardent devotion burns hotter and keeps its heat year after year.

zealous vs. ardent: Zealous is stronger than ardent: ardent passion burns steadily within the person, while zeal boils over into pressing the cause on everyone else.

Which word fits?

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — ard: to burn (Latin ardere)

Suffix — -ent: in a state of; doing

Put it together: Ardent comes straight from Latin ardens, the present participle of ardere, 'to burn' — so an ardent person is, literally, one on fire. English first used it of things actually burning ('ardent flames') before the heat moved inward to describe blazing enthusiasm and devotion. The same root smolders in ardor and in arson.

Use the root in a new word: ardor: Dr. Okonkwo has studied tide pools for forty years, and her colleagues say her ardor is undimmed.

Word Choice

strong, sincere — approving heat, no verdict of excess

Ardent admires the flame without accusing it. That sets it apart from this unit's over-the-line words: adulation is gushing that outruns reason, and idolatrous devotion has turned a person into a god, but an ardent supporter burns hot while keeping their judgment. Watch the upper boundary too — when the fire starts getting pushed on other people, English reaches for zealous instead.
